newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.
newsitem.headline: AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.

text.p: Australian Meat and Livestock Corp's (AMLC) weekly export prices are as follows:
AUSTRALIAN EXPORT PRICES TO U.S. IN U.S. CENTS/LB, CIF.
Bull (95 Chemical Lean) 87 -4 on last week
AUSTRALIAN EXPORT PRICES TO JAPAN IN U.S. CENTS/LB CIF.
Chilled grassfed fullsets 123 -4 on last week

AMLC COMMENTARY: Cattle prices generally increased this week, defying trends in beef export markets. Supplies of cattle tightened further across southern Australia, apparently the principal factor underlying price rises. Yardings in New South Wales (NSW) were 18,884 head, five percent less than last week and 13 percent less than two weeks ago. In Victoria, yardings totalled 9,788 head, seven percent less than last week and 20 percent less than a fortnight ago. Slaughterings in NSW last week totalled 41,788 head, a reduction of nine percent.

Low cattle supplies, as well as following usual seasonal patterns, in part reflected dry weather conditions in Victoria and southern NSW through late summer and spring. Forced sales in that period are, to an extent, choking current supplies. Additionally, grain planting is now well underway in many areas.

In contrast to NSW and Victoria, cattle supplies in Queensland are still plentiful. Yardings this week in Queensland totalled 20,530 head, up 4,756 head. The Queensland kill last week was 64,724 head, with the female proportion again high at 48.8 percent.

High female slaughterings over the past couple of months may be an indication that some producers are downscaling cattle operations. The recent improvement in wool prices and a rise in optimism for wool is perhaps encouraging a slight switch from beef to wool production. The growth in the live cattle trade also would be impacting upon the composition of the kill, with shipments to Indonesia and the Philippines primarily steers.
Export markets did not share in rising cattle values this week. Chilled grassfed fullsets to Japan sold for about 315 cents a kg, down nine cents a kg on last week.

Beef demand in Japan is normally seasonally soft in June and July, following Golden Week in May and before the northern hemisphere autumn sales campaigns. The rainy season has begun in Japan, resulting in hot sticky weather, and, reportedly, increased quantities of U.S. beef are starting to emerge.

Cattle on feed in the U.S. are nine percent more than at this time last year, with many to be finished in the next two months. Fed cattle in the U.S. this week sold for about US$64 a hundredweight (cwt), a drop of $4-$5 a cwt since early May. Prices are expected to soften a little during the northern summer before rising to about $70 a cwt by year's end.

Export prices for lean Australian grinding beef exported to the U.S. eased further this week, closing at about 194 cents a kg, down 10 cents a kg. Wet weather over the Memorial Day weekend, the apparent failure of McDonald's 55 cents Big Mac promotion and heavy supplies now entering the U.S. are all contributing to the price weakness.

The fed beef chuck market is also depressed because of limited demand at this time of year for pot roasts. These chucks are now moving into ground beef formulas, reducing demand for both 90CL and 50CL grinding meat.

Over the next few months, however, the U.S. manufacturing beef market offers improved prospects, with prices expected to rise moderately. This optimism is driven by more demand for chucks from non-grinding users in late summer, less cow slaughter than a year ago, and lower arrivals from New Zealand.
